title: The Murder of Ish-bosheth
summary: With Abner dead, Ish-bosheth loses heart and Israel is thrown into alarm. Two of his own raiding captains, Rechab and Baanah, murder him in his bed at midday and carry his head to David at Hebron, expecting a reward. David, recalling how he dealt with the Amalekite who claimed to have killed Saul, has them executed for killing a righteous man in his own house, and buries Ish-bosheth's head in Abner's tomb.
story: The house of Saul is collapsing. Its last strong man, Abner, has been murdered (chapter 3), and its king, Ish-bosheth, is left without courage or support. This chapter removes the final obstacle between David and the throne of all Israel, and once again it happens without David's knowledge or command. The narrator is careful to show that David rewards none of the men who try to win his favor by killing his rivals. The chapter repeats the pattern of chapter 1, where an Amalekite brought Saul's crown, and David himself makes the connection. It also pauses to introduce Mephibosheth, Jonathan's lame son, the last male of Saul's line with a claim to the throne. He will be important later, when David seeks to show kindness to Jonathan's house (chapter 9).
historical:
The events come at the end of Ish-bosheth's two-year reign at Mahanaim, east of the Jordan, around the end of the first decade of the tenth century BC (exact dates are uncertain). Rechab and Baanah are from Beeroth, one of the four cities of the Gibeonites who made a treaty with Joshua (Joshua 9:17), later counted as part of Benjamin (Joshua 18:25). The note that the Beerothites fled to Gittaim and have lived there as foreigners to this day suggests some upheaval that drove the original inhabitants out; some interpreters connect this with Saul's attempt to wipe out the Gibeonites (2 Samuel 21:1-2), which might give the brothers a motive against Saul's house, though the text does not say so.

The murderers travel by way of the Arabah, the Jordan Valley, to reach Hebron from Mahanaim, a long night's march. Mephibosheth was five when news came of the defeat at Jezreel (the battle on Gilboa), so he would have been a boy still during Ish-bosheth's reign. First Chronicles 8:34 and 9:40 call him Merib-baal, and, as with Ish-bosheth (Eshbaal), most scholars think the scribes of Samuel replaced the element baal with bosheth, shame.
cultural:
The midday rest during the heat of the day was a normal custom in the Near East, and a house would be quiet then. The murderers enter as if to fetch wheat, perhaps posing as men collecting grain rations, a detail that shows how easily they moved in the king's house. Killing a man on his own bed, in his own house, was regarded as a particularly treacherous act, a violation of the security everyone expected at home.

Bringing an enemy's head to a king was a common way to prove a kill and claim a reward, as David himself had once brought Goliath's head to Saul. David's sentence reflects Israel's law of bloodguilt (Genesis 9:6; Numbers 35), which required the life of a murderer. The mutilation of the bodies (cutting off hands and feet) and their public display by the pool of Hebron was a punishment meant to be seen, marking the hands that killed and the feet that ran with the news. Burying Ish-bosheth's head in Abner's tomb gave him an honorable burial beside the commander who had made him king.
literary: The chapter is framed by weakness (verse 1, Ish-bosheth's hands grow feeble) and justice (verse 12, the murderers' hands are cut off). The story of Mephibosheth (verse 4) interrupts the narrative at a tense moment, just after the killers are introduced and before they strike, and its position makes a point: Saul's house is now represented by a lame child. The murder itself is told twice (verses 5-6 and 7), a device that slows the scene and stresses its brutality. David's speech is the climax. He begins with an oath by the LORD who has redeemed his life, reminding the killers that he has never needed anyone to rescue him by murder, and then argues from the lesser to the greater: if the man who brought news of Saul's death was executed, how much more those who killed a righteous man in his bed.

outline.t: Ish-bosheth loses heart; Rechab and Baanah introduced

doctrines.note: David confesses that the LORD has redeemed his life from all distress. He has not needed to kill anyone to reach the throne, and he refuses to accept the help of those who do. The chapter shows God's purposes reaching their goal without the king's hands being stained.

Murder is punished, even when it serves the interests of the one judging. David applies justice impartially, treating the killing of a rival as seriously as the killing of a friend. Justice in the kingdom is not what benefits the king but what the LORD requires.

David calls Ish-bosheth a righteous man, not because he was a great king but because he had done nothing to deserve murder. Every life bears the image of God (Genesis 9:6), and the life of a political rival is not cheap.

words.note: Padah, to ransom or redeem, used of buying back a person or animal and of God's rescue of Israel from Egypt (Deuteronomy 7:8). David's oath by the LORD, who has redeemed his life from all distress, says that God has been his deliverer through all the years of danger. He does not need murderers to do what God has already done.

Basar, to bring news, especially good news, usually of victory. The Amalekite thought he was a bearer of good news. The Greek translation of this verb (euangelizo) is the word behind gospel, the good news of Christ. Here the news is corrupt, since it is news of a murder, and David refuses it.

Tsaddiq, righteous or innocent. In a legal setting it means not guilty. David calls Ish-bosheth righteous in the sense that he had done nothing to deserve death at the hands of his own men. The word marks his murder as the shedding of innocent blood.

Tsarah, distress or trouble, from a root meaning narrow or tight. David's life had been hemmed in by danger from Saul, from the Philistines, and from his own men at Ziklag. The oath gathers all those narrow places into one confession: the LORD brought him out of every one.

christ: The chapter's link to Christ is in the character of the king God is raising up. David refuses to build his kingdom on the murder of his rivals, and he acknowledges that his rescue has come from the LORD, not from human scheming. The New Testament presents Jesus as the son of David who likewise refused power offered by illegitimate means (Matthew 4:8-10) and whose kingdom was established not by killing his enemies but by dying for them (Romans 5:10). The word for bringing good news in this chapter is the Old Testament root of the word gospel; the chapter shows false good news, the report of a murder, while the gospel of Christ announces the defeat of death itself. These are thematic links, not predictions.

hard.q: Was David's punishment of Rechab and Baanah just, and why were their bodies mutilated?
hard.a: By the standards of Israel's law, the death penalty for premeditated murder was required (Numbers 35:16-21), and these men had killed a sleeping king in his own house. The mutilation and public display are harder for modern readers. In the ancient world such displays were a common way to show the reason for a punishment and to deter others; here the hands that killed and the feet that carried the head were singled out. Deuteronomy 21:22-23 limited the exposure of a hanged body to a single day, and nothing suggests David broke that limit. Some readers see the harsh treatment as political theater, David proving publicly that he had no part in the murder; others as ordinary justice for its time. The text does not present this punishment as a model for all times, but it does show David's determination that the kingdom not be built on innocent blood.

questions: Rechab and Baanah assumed David would reward them for removing a rival. What wrong assumptions do people make about what will please those in power, or about what pleases God?
David confessed that the LORD had redeemed his life from every distress. As you look back, what distresses has God brought you through?
Mephibosheth's injury came from someone else's panic, not his own fault. How do the consequences of others' actions shape a person's life, and where does grace meet them?
